content: Silicon dioxide, also referred to as silica or silox (derived from the Latin term silex), is a chemical compound composed of silicon and oxygen. Its chemical formula is SiO₂. This compound has been recognized for its hardness since the 9th century. In nature, silicon dioxide is most commonly found as sand or quartz and is also present in the cell walls of diatoms. It serves as a fundamental component in the production of glass and materials like concrete. Silicon dioxide is manufactured in various forms, including: Glass, with a high-purity, colorless variant known as fused silica. Synthetic amorphous silica. Silica gel, which is often used as a desiccant in products like new clothing and leather goods. Silicon dioxide is utilized in the production of numerous products: Soda-lime glass, an inexpensive and widely used type of glass, is commonly found in drinking glasses, bottles, and windows. It is a raw material for whiteware ceramics, including earthenware, stoneware, and porcelain. It is a key ingredient in the production of Portland cement. As a food additive, it functions primarily as a flow agent in powdered foods or to absorb moisture. In microelectronics, the natural oxide layer that forms on silicon is highly advantageous. This layer acts as an excellent electrical insulator with high chemical stability. It can protect silicon, store charge, block current, or allow controlled current flow in devices. However, this oxide layer grows very slowly at room temperature. To produce such layers, silicon is typically heated in high-temperature furnaces in an oxygen-rich environment, a process known as thermal oxidation. Silicon dioxide is also used as a raw material for aerogels, such as those employed in the Stardust spacecraft. It plays a role in the extraction of DNA and RNA due to its ability to bind nucleic acids in the presence of chaotropic agents. In medicinal applications, it is added in small amounts to anti-foaming agents like simethicone to enhance their defoaming properties. Hydrated silica is included in toothpaste formulations as an abrasive to help remove plaque. Health Effects Inhaling fine crystalline silica dust over time, even in small quantities (e.g., OSHA permits 0.1 mg/m³), can lead to serious health conditions such as silicosis, bronchitis, or, in rare cases, cancer. This occurs because the dust becomes lodged in the lungs, causing continuous irritation and reducing lung capacity. Silica does not dissolve in the body over time. Vulnerable populations, such as children, asthmatics, allergy sufferers, and the elderly, may experience adverse effects more quickly due to their reduced lung capacity. When ingested orally, silicon dioxide passes through the gastrointestinal tract unchanged and is excreted in the feces without leaving any trace. Small pieces of silicon dioxide are harmless unless they are large enough to cause mechanical obstruction or sharp enough to damage the gastrointestinal lining. Silicon dioxide does not produce fumes, is insoluble in the body, and has no nutritional value or toxicity. Chemistry Silicon dioxide forms when silicon is exposed to oxygen or air. A very thin layer of native oxide, approximately 1 nanometer thick, develops on silicon surfaces under ambient conditions. To grow controlled layers of silicon dioxide, higher temperatures (600–1200°C) and specific environments are used. For instance, dry oxidation involves O₂, while wet oxidation uses H₂O. The thickness of the silicon consumed during oxidation is about 44% of the thickness of the resulting silicon dioxide layer. Alternative methods for depositing silicon dioxide layers include: Low-temperature oxidation (LTO) of silane. Decomposition of tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) at 680–730°C. Plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) using TEOS at approximately 400°C. Pyrogenic silica, also known as fumed silica or silica fume, is a fine particulate form of silicon dioxide. It is produced by burning silicon tetrachloride (SiCl₄) in an oxygen-rich hydrocarbon flame, resulting in a smoke of SiO₂. Quartz, a crystalline form of silicon dioxide, exhibits maximum solubility in water at around 340°C. This property is exploited in hydrothermal processes to grow single quartz crystals. Over 1–2 months, crystals weighing 0.5–1 kg can be grown, providing a source of highly pure quartz for electronic applications. Fluorine reacts with silicon dioxide to form silicon tetrafluoride (SiF₄) and oxygen (O₂), while other halogens (chlorine, bromine, iodine) react less readily. Hydrofluoric acid (HF) attacks silicon dioxide to produce hexafluorosilicic acid (H₂SiF₆). This reaction is utilized in the semiconductor industry to remove or pattern silicon dioxide layers. Silicon dioxide dissolves in hot concentrated alkali or fused hydroxides, reacting with basic metal oxides (e.g., sodium oxide, potassium oxide, lead(II) oxide, zinc oxide) to form silicates and glasses. For example, the reaction between sodium oxide and SiO₂ can yield sodium orthosilicate, sodium silicate, or various types of glass, depending on the reactant proportions. Commercially significant glasses, such as soda-lime glass, borosilicate glass, and lead glass, are formed through these processes. In these glasses, silica acts as the network or lattice former. At high temperatures, silicon reacts to produce gaseous silicon monoxide (SiO). Structure and Properties Silicon dioxide exists in several crystalline forms as well as amorphous forms. Most crystalline forms consist of tetrahedral SiO₄ units linked by shared vertices in different arrangements. The silicon-oxygen bond length varies among these forms. For instance, in α-quartz, the bond length is 161 pm, while in α-tridymite, it ranges from 154–171 pm. The Si-O-Si bond angle also varies, from 140° in α-tridymite to 180° in β-tridymite. In α-quartz, the angle is 144°. Its density is 4.287 g/cm³, compared to 2. The increased density in stishovite is due to the higher coordination number and longer Si-O bond lengths (176 pm and 181 pm) compared to α-quartz (161 pm). This change in coordination also increases the ionic character of the Si-O bond. Under normal conditions, α-quartz is the only stable crystalline form of silicon dioxide, and impurities in α-quartz can result in various colors. Molecular Forms of Silicon Dioxide Molecular silicon dioxide (SiO₂) can be produced by condensing silicon monoxide (SiO) in an argon matrix cooled with helium, along with oxygen atoms generated by microwave discharge. This molecular form has a linear structure, with a Si-O bond length of 148.3 pm, shorter than the 161 pm bond length in α-quartz. The bond energy is estimated at 621.7 kJ/mol. Dimeric silicon dioxide, (SiO₂)₂, can be synthesized by reacting oxygen with matrix-isolated dimeric silicon monoxide (Si₂O₂). In this dimer, two oxygen atoms bridge the silicon atoms, forming an Si-O-Si angle of 94° and a bond length of 164.6 pm. The terminal Si-O bond length is 148.2 pm.
